slot.brief: Field from potential: a given potential function V(x,y) or potential along a line; differentiate to get the field and evaluate the vector direction at a specified point.

stem: The potential is $V(x,y)=(x^2+2xy)\ \text{V m}^{-2}$, where $x$ and $y$ are in metres. What is the electric field at $(1\ \text{m},1\ \text{m})$?

verdicts.working: \(\mathbf E=-\nabla V\). At \((1,1)\), \(\partial V/\partial x=4\,\text{V m}^{-1}\) and \(\partial V/\partial y=2\,\text{V m}^{-1}\), so \(\mathbf E=(-4\hat{\mathbf i}-2\hat{\mathbf j})\,\text{V m}^{-1}\).

working:
$\vec E=-\nabla V$
$E_x=-\dfrac{\partial V}{\partial x}=-(2x+2y),\quad E_y=-\dfrac{\partial V}{\partial y}=-2x$
At $x=y=1\ \text{m}$: $\vec E=(-4\hat{\mathbf{i}}-2\hat{\mathbf{j}})\ \text{V m}^{-1}$.

Independent check: \(\mathbf E=-\nabla V\). At \((1,1)\), \(\partial V/\partial x=4\,\text{V m}^{-1}\) and \(\partial V/\partial y=2\,\text{V m}^{-1}\), so \(\mathbf E=(-4\hat{\mathbf i}-2\hat{\mathbf j})\,\text{V m}^{-1}\).
solution:
The electric field is the negative gradient of the potential:
$$\vec E=-\nabla V=-(2x+2y)\hat{\mathbf i}-2x\hat{\mathbf j}.
$$
At $(x,y)=(1,1)$, $\vec E=(-4\hat{\mathbf i}-2\hat{\mathbf j})\,\text{V m}^{-1}$.
